source.title: Efficiently Seeking Flat Minima for Better Generalization in Fine-Tuning Large Language Models and Beyond
source.authors: Jia-Xin Deng; Qingcheng Zhu; Jun-Biao Pang; Lin-Lin Yang; Zhong-Qian Fu; Bao-Chang Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sharpness-aware LoRA fine-tuning to language and vision-language models and reports downstream performance, extending sharpness/generalization work to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. It does not directly test the listed versions’ specific behaviors.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream benchmark results for EFMLoRA and related methods. Those results concern generalization performance, but do not measure training-to-test error gaps, random-label memorization, widening past interpolation, or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization premise to design FMLoRA and EFMLoRA and evaluates their downstream performance. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of training–test gaps, or any other listed version. Sharpness approximation and balancedness measurements do not establish that relationship.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: FMLoRA and its efficient EMA variant seek flatter minima, and EFMLoRA often matches or improves downstream performance relative to LoRA and full fine-tuning with modest overhead. The authors interpret this as evidence linking reduced sharpness to better PEFT generalization. This is their interpretation; the paper does not directly measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap correlation, and performance improvements are not universal across settings.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sharpness-aware optimization in LoRA fine-tuning, transferring perturbations from full parameter space into a low-rank subspace and using EMA to reduce overhead; the listed versions concern other interventions or specific measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The perturbation size ρ changes Qwen-VL-Chat results by task: ρ=0.2 is best on ScienceQA and ρ=0.05 performs better on VizWiz. Balancedness patterns vary by layer. EMA sharpness-difference trajectories are reported separately for six datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: EFMLoRA improves the reported RoBERTa aggregate scores over LoRA from 80.0 to 82.3 in few-shot evaluation and from 88.4 to 89.4 on GLUE. Qwen-VL-Chat performance depends on radius: ScienceQA peaks at 91.6 with ρ=0.2, while VizWiz peaks at 51.7 with ρ=0.05; some settings score below LoRA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness-aware LoRA fine-tuning can improve downstream benchmark performance, with benefits depending on task and perturbation radius.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report decreasing absolute differences between EMA-based and SAM-based sharpness during training across six datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EMA perturbations increasingly approximate SAM's perturbation-based loss measurement during the tested fine-tuning runs.

fits_no_version.finding: FMLoRA balancedness decreases in the first query layer, decreases then increases in the twelfth, and increases in the twenty-fourth; the authors report generally lower values than Adam in most layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FMLoRA changes low-rank factor balancedness in a layer-dependent manner.

record.problems: The reported evaluations use downstream benchmark metrics and do not report training-to-test error gaps, so they do not directly establish a relationship between sharpness and the gap specified in the claim. Some baseline results in Tables 1–3 are cited from prior work. Figure 3 and Figure 4 results are described qualitatively, without numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 dataset-level scores and Table 2 dataset-level scores were not extracted as separate rows; aggregate averages were retained. Table 3 reports multiple generation metrics for GPT-2 Medium and Large, and Table 4 reports five datasets across three shot counts; those results were left out because they are downstream metric comparisons that do not measure the claim versions, and extracting them would not add direct evidence about the claimed training-to-test gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets; AdamW is a base optimizer rather than a tested comparison.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions; CLIP uses fixed dropout without an ablation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, training–test gaps among comparably fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus equally sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed against the listed claim versions, so unrelated benchmark improvements cannot receive observed, partial, absent, or reversed states. The study is not an original source for any version. No additional result testing a listed version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep or test-error behavior past zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD or momentum SGD.
No large- versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
The paper studies sharpness-aware LoRA, but does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness against training-to-test gaps among networks with similarly low training loss.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned with EFMLoRA and evaluated on six classification datasets; reports aggregate average score.

rows.note: The paper reports this as an average across the six datasets; it is a downstream score, not a training-to-test error gap.

rows.operation_detail: Measured absolute difference between sharpness computed using EMA perturbations and original SAM perturbations during training.

conditions.value: SNLI, SST-2, SST-5, MNLI, RTE, TREC

rows.measure: Absolute sharpness difference over training iterations
rows.note: The text says the difference consistently decreases across all six datasets; this measures EMA approximation to SAM sharpness, not a training-to-test gap.
rows.check: The decreasing difference between two perturbation-based loss measurements evaluates EMA approximation to SAM. It does not measure V7's sharpness–gap relationship.

rows.subject: RoBERTa-large FMLoRA
rows.operation_detail: Measured balancedness during training across three query layers and compared with Adam.
rows.note: The text says balancedness may increase or decrease across layers, and that FMLoRA generally maintains lower balancedness than Adam in most layers. This is not a measured training-to-test gap.
rows.check: Layerwise balancedness is neither held-out performance nor magnitude-aware sharpness correlated with a training–test gap. Its comparison with Adam does not test V4's optimizer generalization claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
